rules: Import `ruststream::prelude::*` in a service, or the broker crate's own prelude, which re-exports it; the broker and the codec stay explicit choices.

Declare a handler as an `async fn` under `#[subscriber(..)]` whose first parameter is `&T` for one message or `&[T]` for a batch; mount it with `b.include(handler)` inside `with_broker`, and a batch handler with `.batch(n)`.

A reply type derives `Outgoing`: `#[outgoing(name = "..")]` fixes its destination and the subscriber writes the bare `reply`; a type without a name takes `reply("dest")` at the mount site, never both (a declared name wins, and startup warns about the ignored mount-site one).

Publish from inside a handler through an `Out(out): Out<impl Publisher>` parameter bound at the mount site with `.out(marker, policy).build()`; a handler signature never names a broker's publisher type.

The codec is chosen at the mount site (`with_broker_codec`, `Router::with_codec`, `.out_reply(policy).codec(..)`), never per message type; a type that is its own encoding derives `Serialized` or `Deserialized` and needs no codec.

A value a broker's delivery already holds (a row a database driver read) reaches a handler as `&T`, or `&[T]` for a batch, once the broker crate's derive puts `T` on that lane: the type derives `Clone` and not `Deserialize`, a batch of them mounts with no reply and no `Out` slots, and a test asserts it with `with_value` and `received_values`, not `with`.
Cap redeliveries at the mount site with `.max_attempts(n)` and `.dead_letter(name)` right after `include`; `.out_retry(policy)` only replaces the publisher the retry copy leaves through.

Test a service by handing its production app to `ruststream::testing::TestApp::start` (the broker crate's `testing` feature runs each broker in process) and address a broker by its production type, `tb.broker::<KafkaBroker>()`; `TestApp::start_live` runs the same test body against a running stand; do not mock the broker traits or build a second app for tests.
Generate `main` with `#[ruststream::app]` and run the service with `cargo run -- run`; use `start()` only when the service runs beside another server such as an HTTP framework.

Give a handler that computes its own threads with `threads(n)` (or `threads(n, by_key)`) instead of `spawn_blocking` or `rayon` inside the handler, keep `workers(n)` for I/O-bound concurrency, keep in mind that such a handler's leftovers (spawned tasks, `and_after`, `after(..)`, `retry_after` timers) stay on its thread and send work to the app's runtime only through `spawn` or `run` on `Ctx<MainRuntime>`, and size the app's runtime for I/O with `#[ruststream::app(flavor = "current_thread")]` or `worker_threads = n`.

To find the handlers that belong on `threads(n)`, turn on the `poll-diagnostics` feature: every subscription then samples its handler's time in `poll` and warns past the threshold; tune it with `RustStream::poll_diagnostics(PollDiagnostics::new().threshold(..).sample_every(..))` before `with_broker`, and export it with `Metrics::observe_poll_diagnostics` or `Otel::observe_poll_diagnostics`.
Broker-specific settings live on the broker crate's subscription descriptor and publish policy, in that crate's vocabulary; the core exposes none.

A broker crate's own mount step reads the subscription's concurrency, batch size and name off the settings builder (`dispatch()`, `batch_size()`, `subscription_name()`) instead of a setting of its own that repeats `workers(n)`, `threads(n)` or `batch(n)`.

Use `ruststream-sqlx` for a transactional outbox over any RustStream broker and for task queues in the service's own Postgres, MySQL/MariaDB or SQLite tables; its repository README at https://github.com/powersemmi/ruststream-sqlx#readme is the guide.

A transform that names a destination per delivery reads the address with `HeaderMap::get_shared` and passes the `Str` to `Outgoing::set_name`, so the name shares the delivery's buffer instead of being copied out of it.
Misuse is rejected at compile time by design: read the compiler error, it names the missing derive, the unbound slot or the wrong position; do not work around it with runtime checks.

Check what a change costs per message with `just bench --baseline=main`: it counts instructions and allocations per delivery on the core's own scenarios, reports more than two percent more instructions or an allocation above a scenario's declared floor as a failure, and its numbers are the ones a pull request cites.
Open a pull request as a draft and leave it a draft until the maintainer marks it ready for review: CI runs nothing on a draft, so its time is spent once, on the work the maintainer wants checked.
